drivingQuestion: What does the rule that heirs pay a deceased vower's valuation prove about collecting oral and Torah-written debts from heirs?
outcomeNote: Both proposed inferences are blocked and the asymmetry between valuation and assessment is explained by מחוסר אומדנא.

segments.he: גְּמָ׳ תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: חוֹמֶר בַּנְּדָרִים מִבַּעֲרָכִין, שֶׁהַנְּדָרִים חָלִין עַל בְּהֵמָה חַיָּה וָעוֹף, וְאֵין נִדּוֹנִים בְּהֶשֵּׂג יָד, מָה שֶׁאֵין כֵּן בָּעֲרָכִין.
segments.en: «GEMARA:» «The Sages taught» in a baraita: There are halakhot that are more «stringent with regard to vows» of assessment «than with regard to valuations, as vows» of assessment «take effect with regard to a domesticated animal, an undomesticated animal, and a bird.» If one says: It is incumbent upon me to donate the assessment of this bird, he must donate that assessment. This is not the case with regard to valuations, as they do not take effect with regard to animals and birds. «And» another halakha that is more stringent with regard to vows of assessment than with regard to valuations is that the destitute who take vows of assessment «are not assessed based on affordability. This is not the case with regard to valuations,» which are assessed based on whether the one who vows can afford to pay what they vowed.

segments.he: חוֹמֶר בָּעֲרָכִין מִבַּנְּדָרִים, כֵּיצַד? אָמַר: ״עֶרְכִּי עָלַי״ וָמֵת — יִתְּנוּ יוֹרְשִׁין, ״דָּמַי עָלַי״ וָמֵת — לֹא יִתְּנוּ יוֹרְשִׁין, שֶׁאֵין דָּמִים לַמֵּתִים.
segments.en: There is a halakha that is more «stringent with regard to valuations than with regard to vows» of assessment. «How so?» In the case of one who «said:» It is incumbent «upon me» to donate «my valuation, and dies,» his «heirs must give» his valuation to the Temple treasury. But one who says: It is incumbent «upon me» to donate «my assessment, and dies,» his «heirs» need «not give» his assessment to the Temple treasury, «as there is no monetary» value «for the dead.»

segments.he: אָמַר ״עֶרְכִּי עָלַי״ וָמֵת — יִתְּנוּ יוֹרְשִׁין. שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ מִלְוָה עַל פֶּה גּוֹבֶה מִן הַיּוֹרְשִׁין? שָׁאנֵי הָכָא, דְּמִלְוָה כְּתוּבָה בַּתּוֹרָה הִיא.
segments.en: The baraita taught with regard to a person who «said:» It is incumbent «upon me» to donate «my valuation, and dies,» that his «heirs must give» his valuation to the Temple treasury. The Gemara suggests one can «conclude from» this ruling that «one collects a loan by oral agreement from the heirs,» as no promissory note was written with regard to this obligation. The Gemara rejects this conclusion: «Here» the heirs’ obligation to pay the valuation of the deceased «is different,» i.e., it is not the same as a loan by oral agreement, «as» a valuation «is» considered «a loan,» i.e., debt, «written in the Torah,» in accordance with the deceased’s age and sex at the time of the vow.

segments.he: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ: מִלְוָה הַכְּתוּבָה בַּתּוֹרָה כִּכְתוּבָה בִּשְׁטָר דָּמְיָא? הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן — כְּשֶׁעָמַד בַּדִּין.
segments.en: The Gemara objects: If so, can one «conclude from» the baraita that «a loan that is written in the Torah,» i.e., any financial obligation that applies by Torah law, «is considered» as though «it were written in a document?» The Gemara rejects this conclusion: «Here we are dealing with» a case «where he stood in judgment» before he died, and the court obligated him to donate his valuation. The court’s ruling is considered like a financial obligation written in a document, and therefore the heirs are required to pay his valuation.

segments.he: דִּכְוָותַהּ גַּבֵּי ״דָּמַי עָלַי״ שֶׁעָמַד בַּדִּין, אַמַּאי לֹא יִתְּנוּ יוֹרְשִׁין ״דָּמַי עָלַי״? מְחוּסַּר אוּמְדָּנָא. ״עֶרְכִּי עָלַי״ — לֹא מְחוּסָּר וְלֹא כְלוּם.
segments.en: The Gemara asks: If so, then «in the corresponding» situation, «with regard to» one who said: It is incumbent «upon me» to donate «my assessment,» the baraita must also be referring to one «who stood in judgment.» But in that case, «why don’t the heirs have to donate» his assessment? The Gemara answers that in the case of one who said: It is incumbent «upon me» to donate «my assessment,» even if he stood in judgment and the court obligated him to pay, «the assessment» of the precise amount he must pay is still «lacking,» as that amount is determined only through the assessment of a court. By contrast, with regard to one who said: It is incumbent «upon me» to donate «my valuation,» if he stood in judgment and the court obligated him to pay, «nothing is lacking,» as the amount he pays is fixed by the Torah.

moves.summary: brings the baraita expanding the mishna's rubric of stringencies
moves.about: bringing the baraita that lists the stringencies of vows of assessment over valuations and their converse

moves.summary: the baraita's converse clause, on heirs paying a valuation but not an assessment

moves.cueHe: שמע מינה מלוה על פה גובה מן היורשין?
moves.summary: infers that an oral loan is collected from heirs
moves.about: whether the baraita's ruling that heirs pay a vowed valuation shows that an oral loan is collected from heirs

moves.cueHe: שאני הכא, דמלוה כתובה בתורה היא
moves.summary: rejects the inference: a valuation is a debt written in the Torah, not an oral loan
moves.about: whether the valuation debt is an ordinary oral loan — it is not, being a loan written in the Torah

moves.cueHe: שמע מינה: מלוה הכתובה בתורה ככתובה בשטר דמיא?
moves.summary: infers instead that a Torah debt is like a documented debt
moves.about: whether the baraita then shows that a debt written in the Torah is treated as a debt written in a document

moves.summary: rejects that too by narrowing the baraita to one who stood in judgment
moves.about: narrowing the baraita's heirs ruling to one who stood in judgment before he died, so no general rule about Torah debts follows

moves.cueHe: דכוותה גבי ״דמי עלי״ שעמד בדין, אמאי לא יתנו יורשין?
moves.summary: presses the parallel: why then are the heirs of an assessment vower exempt?
moves.about: why, on that reading, the heirs of one who vowed ״דמי עלי״ and stood in judgment are nonetheless exempt

moves.summary: answers that an assessment still lacks its appraisal while a valuation lacks nothing
moves.about: a vow of assessment still lacks the appraisal that fixes the sum, while a valuation is fixed by the Torah and lacks nothing
